title: Still Familiar After 4,500 Years: 25 Visual Echoes of Sindhu-Saraswati Life
excerpt: Bangles, sindoor, dice, carts, pottery and sacred trees: explore 25 visual comparisons between the Harappan world and later South Asian life, beginning with B. B. Lal’s archaeological examples.
html:
A bangle-covered arm, a rounded water pot, a pair of dice, a field crossed by furrows: some of the most vivid encounters with Harappan civilization begin with something that still looks familiar. This visual journey brings together 25 examples of lasting practices, recurring forms and cultural connections.

B. B. Lal’s 2010 address supplies the starting point. Museum photographs, excavation records and later scenes broaden the comparison across present-day India and Pakistan. Most ancient objects here belong to the third millennium BCE; each later image is labelled separately. Click a picture to enlarge it on this page. [1]

Look closely at what persists: a material, a tool, a bodily gesture or a way of working. The images bring ancient objects and later practices side by side, from ornaments and games to farming, craft and sacred imagery.

Gestures, symbols and familiar scenes

1. Hands brought together

The National Museum describes a terracotta male from Harappa as seated in a namaskar pose. Other small figurines also bring their arms and hands toward the chest. Beside a later namaste greeting, the resemblance in the position of the hands and body is immediate. [1, p. 10; 12]

2. The pipal tree as an important image

Pipal-like leaves and trees appear on Indus objects. A later living pipal at a temple in Chhindwara provides the botanical counterpart to the seal image. The tree’s place in South Asian sacred landscapes brings the ancient imagery alongside a familiar living presence. [10, 15]

3. The swastika motif

The swastika appears among Indus seal designs and continues to be used as an auspicious sign in several South Asian religious traditions. The two photographs show the ancient motif and a later Hindu festival setting, placing its recurring form side by side. [1, pp. 2–3; image records]

4. Seated postures, yoga and the Pashupati interpretation

The seal conventionally called Pashupati shows a horned figure seated in a distinctive posture, surrounded by animals. Lal identifies it with Shiva and sees evidence for ancient yoga. A photograph of padmasana in a later yoga class and a modern image of Shiva as a yogi place the seated postures and sacred imagery alongside his comparison. [1, pp. 1–2, 9; 10]

5. Crossed furrows at Kalibangan

Here the comparison records work done on the land. Lal’s excavation photograph shows an Early Harappan field with two sets of furrows at right angles; his later photograph shows similar ploughing near Kalibangan. He reports spacings of about 1.9 metres and 30 centimetres. Lal and excavator B. K. Thapar interpret the pattern as mixed cropping, comparing it with the cultivation of mustard and pulses. [1, pp. 10–12; 2]

6. A bird, a vessel and the thirsty-crow story

Lal reads this painted Lothal vessel as a version of the thirsty-crow tale. His illustration places a bird, a vessel and an antlered animal within the scene. The later Aesop illustration shows how familiar the crow-and-pitcher story became across cultures. Placed together, the images bring the ancient scene and the later illustrated tale into view. [1, pp. 8–9]

What people wear

7. Bangles stacked along the arm

Look first at the left arm of the bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, dated to about 2500 BCE. Its many bangles make a striking comparison with the ornaments worn by Rabari women in Rajasthan. Lal also points to an earlier spiral ornament from Kunal. Together, these examples show the long history of ornaments stacked along the arm. [1, pp. 4–6]

8. Red pigment in the parting of the hair

Lal’s Nausharo example is unusually specific. The painted figurines, which he dates to about 2800–2600 BCE, have black hair and red pigment at the central parting. He compares this with sindoor. The colour and its position make the parallel worth seeing at close range. [1, pp. 3–4]

9. A conical ornament on the head

This is Lal’s own comparison plate: a gold cone from Mohenjo-daro alongside a later bridal head ornament, partly covered by a dupatta. He relates the form to practices in Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana. The photographs place the ornaments side by side for a close view of their shape and placement. [1, pp. 4–5]

10. A pocket-sized grooming kit

Lal placed a copper set attributed to Harappa beside a modern three-in-one kit bought in Aligarh. The two sets combine small implements for personal grooming. In a 2023 commentary on the excavation photograph, Jonathan Mark Kenoyer suggested a later date for the Harappa set, associating it with brick-removal workers. The Punjabi portrait documents the later ear-cleaning profession. [1, p. 6; 13]

Play, toys and stories

11. Cubical dice marked with dots

The ancient dice need little introduction: a small cube, marked faces, and the suspense of a throw. Harappan examples make a clear formal comparison with modern dice. Their cubical shape and dotted faces bring a familiar piece of gaming equipment into view across the millennia. [1, p. 7]

12. Playing pieces and board games

Indus sites have yielded small objects interpreted as gaming pieces. A later pachisi board illustrates how a board, movable counters and chance come together in South Asian play. Lal followed S. R. Rao in comparing Lothal pieces with chess. The objects and board show the enduring place of counters, moves and shared play. [1, p. 8]

13. Animals that move on little wheels

A miniature animal becomes a different kind of object when wheels let it roll. The Indus examples show that makers explored this idea thousands of years ago. The later Channapatna toys show an enduring South Asian interest in small, brightly worked playthings: miniature worlds made for handling and play. [5, 11]

14. Birds modelled in clay

Birds were among the animals shaped by Harappan potters, and some ancient bird-shaped objects were whistles. Later South Asian terracotta birds make a pleasing visual comparison. The use of clay to give familiar creatures a small, portable form has a long history. [11]

Work, food and everyday craft

15. Bullock carts

Harappan terracotta cart models preserve decisions about wheels, an axle, a load and animal traction. Kenoyer documents the long persistence of effective cart designs in India and Pakistan. The bronze shown here comes from Daimabad; its precise date and cultural affiliation are disputed. The later clay toy and the Madhya Pradesh cart extend the visual sequence through later settings. [5, 17]

16. The distinctive humped bull

The shoulder hump and heavy neck make zebu cattle recognizable in ancient art and living herds. The Indus bull figure and the animal photographed in Haridwar put that resemblance before our eyes, showing the long presence and cultural visibility of cattle. [6; image records]

17. The potter’s turning wheel

The wheel helps a potter raise an even wall from prepared clay, repeating a controlled movement until the vessel takes shape. Archaeological work documents wheel-made pottery in the Indus tradition. The present-day potter provides a living view of that operation and the shared craft principle. [6]

18. The rounded earthen water pot

Set the Nausharo vessel beside the later village matka: a swelling body holds the water and a narrower opening helps manage it. Lal’s interest in ordinary things fits this comparison especially well. What persists here is an established earthenware vessel tradition and a familiar household solution. [Image records]

19. Patterned surfaces: geometry passed through the hand

Early Harappan pottery carries bands, intersecting circles, plant forms and other repeating designs. The later ajrak textile shows how geometry also organizes a patterned surface in Sindh. Bands, repeated shapes and carefully arranged motifs connect the visual language of these decorated surfaces. [14]

20. Grinding with stone against stone

The movement is simple and demanding: ingredients on the lower stone, a handheld stone moving over them. Harappan grinding equipment and a later sil-batta make a close functional comparison. CSMVS’s catalogue explicitly notes that similar grinding stones remain in use in rural India. [7]

21. Cloth made from prepared fibres

Organic textiles usually survive poorly. This mineralized fragment from Nausharo is valuable because it preserves a physical trace of woven cloth. Compare it with the much later illustration of cotton and textile work observed in India in the 1790s. The images connect us with the long importance of fibre preparation, thread and weaving. [8; image records]

22. Metal cast through a wax model

The Dancing Girl also belongs to the history of lost-wax metal casting. Wax gives the desired shape, a mould is formed around it, and metal takes the place of the removed wax. Dhokra artisans continue to work with lost-wax processes, carrying this technological principle into living craft. [6, 9]

Other familiar forms

23. White shell bracelets

Harappan craftspeople cut bangles from large marine shells, bringing coastal materials far inland. Excavated burials show that shell bangles were actually worn. Compare these with the white shankha bracelets worn by Bengali brides today. The material and the form of an arm circlet connect the two images. [3]

24. Bead necklaces and the craft behind them

The necklaces and loose beads show another durable pleasure: combining polished stones into something worn on the body. Harappan artisans drilled, shaped and polished materials including carnelian, agate and steatite. Studies of bead-making at Khambhat in Gujarat have helped archaeologists understand ancient production through the work of living craftspeople. [3, 4]

25. A well built as a ring

A circular brick well from Mohenjo-daro and a much later well in Rajasthan show the persistence of drawing groundwater through a lined shaft. A ring of masonry, access from above and water drawn for a settlement bring a familiar arrangement into view across the centuries. [16; image records]

What these images carry forward

Continuity comes into view through particular details: a shell turned into a bracelet, a bead drilled through its centre, a cart designed for animal traction, clay raised on a wheel. Across these 25 comparisons, ancient objects sit beside later ornaments, tools, gestures and sacred images.

Together, they bring the everyday world of the past closer: things people wore, made, played with and passed on.

title: What Ashoka Wanted His People to Hear: A Journey Through His Edicts
excerpt: Follow Ashoka’s messages through time: from the suffering of Kalinga to daily kindness, accountable officials and the hope that persuasion could outlast a king.
html:
What did Ashoka want someone standing before one of his inscriptions to take home? Follow his messages through time and a conversation unfolds: about the cost of conquest, the effort of becoming better, and the responsibilities shared by a ruler and his people.

Eight years after consecration: remember what conquest costs

Major Rock Edict XIII, written later, looks back to the conquest of Kalinga eight years after consecration. It reports 150,000 people deported, 100,000 killed and many times that number dead.

These are the inscription’s figures, not independently verified casualty totals. Their purpose in the text is unmistakable: the king’s success is made to carry the weight of human devastation.

The passage then moves beyond the battlefield. It describes the grief of friends, relatives and companions when someone they love is killed or taken away. People who survive a conquest still suffer through the suffering of others. The inscription makes that emotional chain part of the reckoning.

Ashoka goes on to praise conquest through dhamma. Even here, the voice remains royal, claiming influence across frontiers and looking toward the conduct of future heirs. Remorse becomes a principle of government and a claim about how the dynasty should continue. The edict gives us a public statement of regret; it cannot give us unmediated access to the king’s private mind.

Ten years after consecration: change what a royal journey is for

Major Rock Edict VIII recalls a visit to Sambodhi ten years after consecration. It describes tours of dhamma: visiting religious practitioners, giving to them, supporting the aged, and discussing conduct with people in the countryside. Earlier royal pleasure tours had included hunting.

The message to his people is that a king’s presence should bring help and conversation about how to live. Ashoka presents his own journeys as an example of changed priorities.

Early personal appeals: improvement is open to everyone

The First Minor Rock Edict belongs to the early appeals, though its exact place in this sequence is uncertain. Ashoka recalls more than two and a half years as a Buddhist lay follower, with stronger effort only later. He urges both high and low to exert themselves. The encouragement is personal: moral progress requires practice, and rank does not reserve it for the powerful. These relative dates do not establish an instant conversion after Kalinga.

Twelve to thirteen years after consecration: make dhamma daily practice

In the later Pillar Edict VI, Ashoka looks back to issuing written instructions for people’s welfare twelve years after consecration. Rock Edict III dates an order for teaching tours to that same point. His appeal is becoming a continuing public programme.

The word dhamma carries a range of meanings, and a single English equivalent can flatten it. In these public messages it often concerns conduct: compassion, restraint, truthfulness, generosity and obligations toward other people.

The edicts repeatedly bring grand ideas into small encounters. How do you treat a servant? What do you owe your parents? What happens when generosity becomes a performance while your behavior remains cruel?

Major Rock Edict III connects instruction with obedience to parents, generosity, avoiding the killing of animals and moderation in expenditure and possessions. Officials are to make five-year tours that combine administrative work with moral teaching.

The scale is striking. A king’s message travels through an empire to arrive at a household, a working relationship or a decision about spending. Dhamma becomes something that can be practised repeatedly, in ordinary situations where nobody is erecting a monument.

By thirteen years after consecration, according to Rock Edict V, he has appointed dhamma-mahamatras. Their responsibilities include different religious groups, the aged, the vulnerable and prisoners. He wants people to understand that moral concern should have officials, duties and practical consequences.

The kitchen appears in Major Rock Edict I. Ashoka describes a reduction in the animals killed for his table and promises to end the remaining slaughter. The detail brings the king’s household under the scrutiny of his own message.

In Major Rock Edict II, the king describes medical arrangements for people and animals, the introduction of useful plants, wells and roadside trees. The reach he claims extends beyond his own territory.

During the rock-edict programme: listen, govern fairly and restrain your speech

Then the writing becomes almost breathlessly administrative. In Major Rock Edict VI, Ashoka says reports should reach him wherever he is: eating, in his inner rooms, travelling or in the parks.

It is an image of kingship built around availability. The people’s business is supposed to interrupt the ruler’s comfort. We cannot measure the actual efficiency of this system from the inscription alone, but we can see the standard of responsibility he chooses to advertise.

The First Separate Rock Edict, addressed to officials in Kalinga, makes the problem sharper. It warns against unjust imprisonment and harsh treatment, and names anger, envy, cruelty, haste, laziness and fatigue as obstacles to fair administration. An official’s bad temper becomes a matter of public consequence.

Its declaration, “All men are my children,” is memorable. Equally revealing are the inspections and instructions surrounding it. Paternal language has to be carried through the machinery of government.

Major Rock Edict XII is one of the most searching texts in the collection. It warns that glorifying one’s own community by attacking others can damage the very community one hopes to exalt. Listening becomes an ethical duty.

The argument still has bite. Religious devotion can become a justification for careless speech; the edict asks what that speech actually does. It encourages learning across communities while allowing people to remain attached to their own.

The message had to cross languages as well as distances. The Kandahar bilingual inscription uses Greek and Aramaic, with differences in wording. The Kalinga instructions also prescribe repeated public hearings. People could encounter the king’s words by listening, even when they could not read them themselves.

Twenty years after consecration: make devotion publicly visible

The Lumbini inscription records Ashoka’s personal visit twenty years after consecration to honour the Buddha’s birthplace. A pillar and favourable tax treatment make devotion visible in a place and its administration; the exact fiscal wording remains debated. His Buddhist commitment continues alongside the broader moral instructions addressed to his subjects.

Twenty-six years after consecration: examine yourself and govern with restraint

Major Pillar Edict II offers a compact definition through qualities and actions: few sins, many good deeds, compassion, liberality, truthfulness and purity. This is a useful place to begin before importing an entire modern political philosophy into the word.

Pillar Edict III asks people to notice their faults as well as their good deeds. In this late pillar programme, personal self-examination sits beside instructions for justice and protection. The message reaches inward to motives and outward to what officials do to other people.

Major Pillar Edict IV asks for impartiality in judicial proceedings and punishment. It also grants a three-day respite to prisoners condemned to death, allowing relatives to intercede or the condemned to make gifts and fast for the next world.

Pause over both halves of that policy. The inscription introduces time, appeal and spiritual preparation into the approach to an execution. It also assumes that executions occur. Compassion operates inside a penal order that the king continues to uphold.

Major Pillar Edict V is more elaborate: protected animals, restrictions on killing, limits on branding and castration, and days when fish must not be sold. Some species identifications remain uncertain. The rules have categories, exceptions and calendar limits; they should not be expanded into a claim that every form of animal killing had been abolished.

Twenty-seven years after consecration: persuasion must outlast the king

Pillar Edict VII dates itself twenty-seven years after consecration. Ashoka reviews proclamations, officers, gifts and public works, asking how people can actually be encouraged to improve. It reads as a royal assessment of the project developed across the earlier messages.

The later Major Pillar Edict VII returns to shade, water, officials and gifts. It also distinguishes moral restrictions from the deeper change that persuasion can bring. A ruler can issue an order; getting people to change their habits is another undertaking.

These are royal claims about provision and intention. They do not independently prove that every promised facility existed everywhere. They do show a conception of rule in which a traveller’s thirst and an animal’s welfare belong in a king’s account of his responsibilities.

He asks that these instructions endure for his descendants and far into the future. His intended audience now includes people who will live after him. The lasting ambition is a habit of conduct that survives the person issuing the orders.

What he wanted people to carry away

Read in this sequence, the messages accumulate: remember suffering; make an effort regardless of rank; practise kindness at home; expect responsibility from officials; speak respectfully across religions; examine your own faults. Later texts return to earlier concerns. This is the king’s account of his aims, and the inscriptions alone cannot tell us how completely his subjects accepted them.

Then open the complete guide to Ashoka’s edicts and inscriptions. Each inscription article brings together an image, original-script material, Roman transliteration, translation and explanation, with the version and sources identified. The next and previous article links let you continue through the collection.

Ashoka’s stones endure because they leave us with a live question: what does power owe to the lives it can injure? His answers contain ambition, discipline, tenderness and contradiction. They repay the effort of reading, one carved argument at a time.

Sources and reading notes

This chronology separates recalled events from the dates of particular instructions or inscriptions. It follows the site versions and historical translations cited in the linked articles; the minor rock texts cannot all be assigned exact positions. Dates and readings vary in scholarship. The next and previous links in the inscription collection follow its catalogue order.

  • E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (1925), Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, volume I.
  • University of Oslo, Bibliotheca Polyglotta Ashoka Library, for texts and translations based on Hultzsch.
  • Harry Falk, Aśokan Sites and Artefacts (2006), for inscriptions, sites and attribution questions.
  • Kandahar image record, Wikimedia Commons.

The dates above count years elapsed after his consecration. Edict numbers are modern labels, not a reading order. An inscription can recall an earlier event; the order of some texts remains uncertain. This is a chronology of the events and messages they describe, with those limits kept visible.
